strengths: Clear and well-motivated architecture: layer-local external memory with bidirectional mem2tok/tok2mem cross-attention and a simple LRU replacement/convex-blend rule is well specified (Algorithms 1-2, Figure 2), easy to reproduce from the text, and modular per layer.

Impressive long-horizon retention results: 100% success on T-Maze up to 1M-step corridors with an attention window of L=10 (S=3), plus perfect length generalization across train/test lengths (Figure 4), directly and convincingly supports the central claim of memory far beyond the native context.

Broad empirical coverage across three distinct benchmarks (T-Maze, 48 POPGym tasks, MIKASA-Robo visual manipulation) with strong baseline suites spanning sequence models (DT, RATE, DMamba, RMT, TrXL) and offline RL (CQL, Diffusion Policy); ELMUR achieves top aggregate POPGym score (10.4) and ~2x gains on several MIKASA-Robo tasks.

Thorough ablation study (RQ5) covering memory size, blend factor, initialization, bias, LRU removal, per-layer vs shared memory, and MoE-vs-MLP FFN, plus a sanity check that memory mechanisms do not hurt fully observable CartPole.

Practical efficiency: bounded memory cost independent of sequence length; reported runtime is faster per step than RATE/DT despite more parameters; full hyperparameter tables (Table 5) and fixed code paths support reproducibility.
Honest limitations section (fixed LRU blending, offline IL only, no real-robot experiments) and a controlled evaluation protocol (multiple seeds, 100 evaluation episodes, SEM reporting).
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the components are well-known individually (Transformer-XL-style segment recurrence, Memformer/Transformer-XL-style memory cross-attention, convex-blend updates akin to exponential moving average, LRU replacement from systems). The contribution is primarily a sensible combination plus the reversal of relative bias in the write path, rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The theoretical analysis is essentially trivial: Propositions 1 and 2 (exponential forgetting under a convex update and boundedness of a convex combination of bounded vectors) follow directly from the update rule; they do not address learning dynamics, retrieval quality, or the interaction between LRU selection and task performance, so the 'theoretical contribution' claim is overstated.

Evaluation is imitation learning only (BC-style supervised losses on expert/offline data); the method is motivated by RL and credit assignment under partial observability, but no online RL experiments are provided, limiting the scope of the central claim about 'long-horizon RL'.

Only 3 (4 for T-Maze) seeds per run, and ablations are confined to a single POPGym task (RememberColor3-v0); intermediate blending (lambda ~0.4-0.6) is reported as unstable, and sensitivity to hyperparameters across suites is not fully characterized.

Some baseline comparisons are incomplete: RMT and TrXL appear in T-Maze but are absent from the MIKASA-Robo and POPGym aggregate tables, making cross-benchmark claims against the closest recurrent-memory competitors harder to verify; POPGym gains over RATE are modest (10.4 vs 9.5).

Detached memory between segments (no backpropagation through time through the memory track) may limit what information can be learned to write into memory; the paper does not analyze or ablate this design choice despite it being a significant training compromise.

Missing or hard-to-find details on some claims, e.g., '100,000x beyond the attention window' mixes training configuration (L=10, S=3) with evaluation length, and the POPGym Table 4 caption references 21 tasks while the benchmark has 48, causing minor internal inconsistencies.

strengths: Broad empirical evaluation across three distinct benchmarks (T-Maze, 48 POPGym tasks, MIKASA-Robo) with a consistent evaluation protocol, multiple runs, and reported standard errors
Strong headline results: 100% success on T-Maze up to one-million-step corridors, near-uniform gains over DT on POPGym, and near-double performance on several MIKASA-Robo tasks
Useful ablation study (memory size, blending factor, relative bias, LRU vs. no LRU, shared vs. per-layer memory) that identifies which components matter
Clear writing and a well-structured method section; Algorithm 1/2 and the LRU figure make the mechanism easy to follow
Includes a CartPole sanity check showing the memory mechanism does not hurt on fully observable MDPs, and reports compute/parameter comparisons with baselines
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is a fairly straightforward combination of existing ingredients — segment-level recurrence (Transformer-XL/RMT), token-memory cross-attention (Memformer, Memorizing Transformers, Neural Map), and a classical LRU cache policy with fixed convex blending (an exponential moving average). The central LRU/blend mechanism is heuristic and unlearned, which weakens the 'memory in deep learning' contribution relative to learned addressing in prior memory-augmented networks

The theoretical analysis (Section 4, Appendix A.1–A.2) is over-sold: Propositions 1 and 2 are elementary inductions on a convex update, and the 'half-life' and boundedness results follow immediately from standard EMA properties. These formal bounds are largely cosmetic and do not constitute a substantive theoretical contribution

Title and framing claim a contribution to RL, but all experiments are offline imitation learning with cross-entropy/MSE losses; no online RL, no RL fine-tuning, and no offline RL method (CQL, Diffusion Policy) is evaluated on POPGym despite being introduced as baselines. The gap between the claimed setting ('Long-Horizon RL') and what is actually evaluated (IL on expert data) is a significant claim–evidence mismatch

Baseline coverage is uneven: CQL, Diffusion Policy, and DMamba appear in the baseline list but are absent from the POPGym aggregation (Table 2) and MIKASA-Robo results; RMT/TrXL appear only in the T-Maze plot. It is unclear whether baselines received comparable per-task hyperparameter tuning to ELMUR (Table 5 shows extensive per-task tuning of ELMUR)

The one-million-step T-Maze result, while striking, may be task-specific: the cue is presented at step 0 and never refreshed, so a model that simply freezes one slot succeeds. The paper does not test memory demands that require selective replacement of intermediate information at extreme horizons, so generality of the '100,000× beyond context' claim is unproven

LRU with fixed blending is acknowledged as a limitation, but the ablation shows performance is highly unstable for intermediate blending (λ≈0.4–0.6) and sensitive to memory initialization σ, suggesting the method requires considerable per-task tuning (visible in Table 5, e.g., LRU blend ranging from 0.01 to 1.0 across tasks), which hurts the 'simple and scalable' narrative

Minor issues: duplicated appendix section titles (A.3 and A.4 both 'Memory-Intensive Environments'), some tables report ±0.00 standard errors, and no code release is stated despite the emphasis on reproducibility

strengths: Clear and well-motivated architecture: layer-local external memory with bidirectional token-memory cross-attention and an LRU-based update rule is a sensible, well-executed combination of known ideas, and the method is described precisely (Algorithms 1-2, equations, relative bias design).

Broad and relevant empirical evaluation across three distinct benchmark families (T-Maze, POPGym-48, MIKASA-Robo) covering synthetic recall, control/puzzles, and visual manipulation, with appropriate baselines spanning sequence models (RMT, TrXL, Dmamba), offline RL sequence models (DT, RATE), and offline RL methods (CQL, DP).

Striking headline result: 100% success on T-Maze with corridor lengths up to 10^6 steps while trained with L=10, S=3, plus strong generalization across training/validation sequence lengths (Figure 4).

Thorough ablation study (RQ5) isolating the contributions of memory size, LRU blending, relative bias, per-layer vs shared memory, and MoE vs MLP FFNs, plus a sanity check that memory does not hurt fully observable CartPole.
Good reproducibility practices: fixed data budgets, seeds, per-task hyperparameters in Appendix Table 5, hardware/evaluation protocol specified, and an honest limitations section.
The analysis connects the blending parameter lambda to a half-life/retention horizon, giving practitioners a usable knob.
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: the components are individually well-established (Transformer-XL segment recurrence, Memformer/Transformer-XL style memory cross-attention, Memformer/NTM-style memory slots, LRU replacement). The contribution is primarily an integration plus the specific LRU convex-blend rule, which is fairly heuristic.

The theoretical analysis (Section 4) is technically trivial: Proposition 1 is a straightforward induction on a geometric decay and Proposition 2 is a one-line triangle inequality. These do not provide meaningful insight about learning dynamics, retrieval quality, or what information is retained—only about the update arithmetic.

Some internal inconsistencies in claims: the abstract/intro state ELMUR is best on 'more than half' / 'top score on 24 of 48' POPGym tasks, but Table 4's caption says 'best performance on 12 tasks'; also 'retention horizons up to 100,000×' derives from a single synthetic task configuration and may overstate generality.

Training uses detached memory between segments (no BPTT through memory), which is a significant limitation the paper does not deeply discuss; it is unclear how well gradient-based learning can shape *what* is written to memory rather than merely what is read, and how this compares to RMT-style truncated BPTT.

Baseline strength on the headline T-Maze experiment is questionable: several baselines collapse to near-random at long horizons (Figure 3), and it is unclear whether they were tuned as carefully as ELMUR (e.g., RMT with longer memory windows).
Offline imitation learning only; no online RL experiments despite the framing around RL, acknowledged but still narrowing the significance of the 'long-horizon RL' claims.
The MoE FFN component is orthogonal to the memory contribution (ablation shows MLP is comparable) yet is baked into the main model, complicating attribution of gains.
Some ablation findings (instability at intermediate lambda, sensitivity when M < N) suggest the method has fragile regimes, but the paper offers limited analysis of why.

strengths: Strong and broad empirical evaluation: T-Maze (100% success up to 1M steps, ~100,000x beyond the attention window), 48 POPGym tasks, 32 MIKASA-Robo manipulation tasks with visual observations, D4RL MuJoCo tasks, and ViZDoom navigation, with a consistent evaluation protocol (multiple seeds, 100 evaluation episodes, SEM reported).

The architecture is well-motivated and clearly specified: per-layer external memory, bidirectional mem2tok/tok2mem cross-attention, relative temporal biases, and an explicit LRU write policy (full replacement then convex blending), summarized in detailed pseudocode (Algorithms 1-2).

Good ablation coverage (RQ5): memory size M vs. required segments, blending factor lambda, initialization sigma, segment configuration, shared vs. layer-local memory, relative bias, LRU, and MoE vs. MLP FFN, with sensible conclusions about capacity dominating performance.

Unusually thorough mechanistic analysis: memory probing with confusion matrices, write/read attention maps, slot update schedules, inter-slot similarity/variance, and PCA analyses that support the claim that performance gains arise from functional memory use rather than added capacity.
Reproducibility is taken seriously: full hyperparameter tables (Table 7), data collection details, hardware setup, anonymous code repository, and a reproducibility statement.

Consistent competitive timing/parameter results (ELMUR faster per step than RATE and DT on T-Maze), and honest inclusion of MDP sanity checks (CartPole, D4RL) showing memory does not hurt fully observable performance.
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: the method is essentially a recombination of known ideas (Transformer-XL/Bulatov segment-level recurrence, Memformer-style global slots, Block-Recurrent Transformer writes, learned read/write cross-attention from NTM/DNC, and convex blend updates similar to Titans). The LRU rule is simple and heuristic; no adaptive/learned write policy is explored.

The theoretical analysis is trivial: Proposition 1 is a geometric-series unrolling of a convex update and Proposition 2 is a one-line triangle-inequality induction. These do not characterize retrieval quality, capacity limits under adversarial writes, or learning dynamics, so the 'formal guarantees' are weak support for the central claims.

Missing strong memory baselines: comparisons omit FFM (Morad et al., 2023b), AMAGO-2, xLSTM, and Titans despite these being cited and directly relevant to memory in POMDP RL; RATE is the only memory-augmented transformer baseline on the robotic suite, and the POPGym comparison set (DT, BC-MLP/LSTM) is weak.

Results are less uniformly dominant than the abstract suggests: on POPGym, ELMUR is not best on Battleship, Concentration, CountRecall, MineSweeper, Autoencode, or several PositionOnly tasks (RATE and BC-LSTM often win); on MIKASA-Robo, several InterceptGrab tasks show negligible gains, and entire task families (BunchOfColors/SeqOfColors/ChainOfColors) score 0.0 for all methods, which is neither discussed nor explained.

Some claims and presentation are inconsistent or overstated: 'nearly doubles' vs. the actual ~1.7x aggregate ratio; 'first on 21 of 23 tasks' vs. Table 8's 32 tasks with 9 tasks at zero for all methods; abstract says 'contributions are twofold' while three are listed; duplicate 'Figure 2, Figure 2' references; missing project page URL in the abstract; D4RL is miscited to Todorov et al. (2012) instead of Fu et al. (2020).

Settings limited to offline imitation learning with expert data; no online RL experiments, no real-robot experiments, and no sim-to-real validation, which narrows the claimed significance for 'real-world robotic agents' as framed in the introduction.

Several findings are underexplored: intermediate lambda (0.4-0.6) instability and the M < N collapse are reported but not explained, and the fixed blending factor is a hand-tuned hyperparameter (Table 7 shows lambda varies wildly across tasks: 0.05-0.9), raising questions about practical tuning cost.

strengths: The proposed architecture is clearly described, with detailed algorithms (Algorithm 1, Algorithm 2), relative-bias formulation, and complete hyperparameter tables (Table 7) supporting reproducibility.

Evaluation is broad, spanning synthetic T-Maze, 48 POPGym tasks, MIKASA-Robo manipulation, D4RL, and ViZDoom, with multiple seeds and a clearly stated evaluation protocol (grand mean ± SEM over runs, 100 evaluation episodes).
The ablation study (RQ5) isolates the contribution of LRU updates, relative bias, per-layer vs. shared memory, memory capacity M, and blending factor λ, showing capacity and LRU dominate.

The memory probing analysis (Appendix A.9–A.11) is a nice addition: confusion matrices, slot-update heatmaps, and attention maps provide evidence that the model actually writes and retains task-relevant information rather than benefiting purely from extra capacity.
The theoretical claims (exponential forgetting, half-life, boundedness) are correct as stated and connect the hyperparameter λ to retention horizons.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: layer-local external memory with read/write cross-attention and slot-wise replacement is a close combination of well-known ingredients (Memformer, Block-Recurrent Transformer, Transformer-XL segment recurrence, LRU slot management). The paper does not clearly articulate what is fundamentally new beyond substituting an LRU write policy.

The theoretical analysis is trivial. Proposition 1 is a standard geometric-series decay of a convex update, the half-life corollary follows immediately, and Proposition 2 is a one-line consequence of convexity and the triangle inequality. Presenting these as 'formal guarantees' and 'theoretical contributions' overstates their significance substantially.

Framing inconsistencies: the title and abstract emphasize 'RL problems', but the method is trained via behavior cloning / imitation on expert demonstrations across all main experiments, and online RL baselines are explicitly excluded. The paper conflates offline sequence modeling, IL, and RL without justifying the RL framing.

Hyperparameter sensitivity is concerning: Table 7 shows very different, finely tuned configurations per task (e.g., LRU blend α from 0.05 to 0.9, memory size from 2 to 256, experts from 1 to 16), and the ablation admits that intermediate λ values are unstable. This undermines the claim of a 'simple and scalable' method and raises questions about per-task tuning effort applied to ELMUR versus baselines.
The ablation study is conducted on a single task (RememberColor3-v0); no evidence is given that component findings transfer to other tasks or domains.

On POPGym and D4RL the improvements are modest (10.4 vs. 9.5 aggregate; 76.4 vs. 78.9/78.5 average on D4RL, where ELMUR is not the top method), and headline claims rely heavily on the synthetic T-Maze extrapolation result, which is a best-case memory-recall scenario.

Some heavy engineering components (DeepSeek-MoE FFNs) are introduced without ablation in the main results; the MoE→MLP ablation shows identical accuracy, so its role in the headline results is unclear and confounds architectural attribution.

Presentation issues undermine polish: the abstract and the code/project-page reference are literally empty ('Code and project page: .'), the contributions bullet list says 'twofold' but lists three items, and repeated broken cross-references appear (e.g., 'LRU rule (Figure 2, Figure 2)').

Writing contains unsupported or imprecise claims (e.g., '100,000× beyond the attention window' derived from a single task setup; 'underscoring reliable credit assignment' in the conclusion without credit-assignment experiments).

Missing comparisons with some closely related memory-augmented sequence models on the robotics benchmark (e.g., Memformer, Block-Recurrent Transformer appear only in related work), making the 'nearly doubles the strongest baseline' claim dependent on a limited baseline set.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across four distinct domains: the synthetic T-Maze (retention up to 1M steps, 100,000x beyond the attention window), all 48 POPGym tasks, the MIKASA-Robo robotic manipulation suite (32 tasks with visual observations), plus supporting D4RL and ViZDoom experiments.

Strong headline results, particularly the near-doubling of baseline performance on MIKASA-Robo (best on 21/23 tasks with nonzero success, ~70% aggregate improvement over RATE) and perfect T-Maze generalization across train/test lengths.

Unusually thorough analysis beyond headline numbers: component ablations (memory size M, blending factor λ, initialization σ, segment configuration, per-layer vs shared memory, relative bias, LRU), memory probing with confusion matrices, update-pattern heatmaps, inter-slot similarity/variance analyses, PCA visualizations, and cross-attention maps that together provide credible mechanistic evidence that the external memory is functionally used.

Well-specified evaluation protocol (3-4 independent runs, 100 evaluation episodes, SEM reporting, matched data budgets and preprocessing across baselines) and a genuine reproducibility effort: full hyperparameter table, pseudocode, and anonymous code release.
Positioning against related work is extensive and honest, with a limitations section (fixed LRU blending, no online RL, no real-robot experiments) that accurately acknowledges scope.
The architecture is clean, simple, and well-motivated; the write-path (tok2mem) plus LRU management is a sensible contrast to read-only cache-style memory like Transformer-XL.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: each ingredient is well established — layer-local memory slots (Memformer), bidirectional token-memory cross-attention (Memformer/Compressive Transformer), relative positional bias (Transformer-XL), segment-level recurrence (RMT), convex blending, and even the OS-style LRU heuristic. The contribution is essentially a careful recombination plus an added LRU write rule, which limits impact.

The theoretical analysis (Section 4) is trivial: Proposition 1 is an induction over a convex update and Proposition 2 is a one-line triangle-inequality argument. Presenting these as 'formal bounds establishing retention horizons and stability' overstates what are textbook-level results and does not illuminate the full architecture (e.g., no analysis of the cross-attention read/write dynamics or training stability).

Missing key baselines on POPGym: the paper compares only to RATE, DT, BC-MLP, and BC-LSTM, omitting strong published POPGym specialists such as FFM (Fast and Forgetful Memory, Morad et al. 2023b — the actual published SOTA on this benchmark, cited in related work but not compared), AMAGO/xLSTM, and other S4/Mamba variants beyond Decision Mamba. Given the modest aggregate margin (10.4 vs 9.5 for RATE), the claim of benchmark superiority is not fully supported.

Some results are spun favorably: on D4RL, ELMUR's average (76.4/74.7) is below TT (78.9) and RATE (78.5), with a suspiciously poor MR Hopper (64.8 vs 91.5 for CQL); on ViZDoom, ELMUR (55.28±0.94) trails RATE (59.21±1.19), yet the text frames both as 'matching' prior best. A more candid discussion of where ELMUR does not win would strengthen the paper.

The ablation study is confined to a single task (RememberColor3-v0), so the generality of conclusions about LRU, λ sensitivity, and instability at intermediate blending (λ≈0.4-0.6) is unverified; notably, the 'optimal' configuration (λ=0, pure replacement) suggests the convex-blending component may add complexity without benefit.
Only 3 seeds per configuration; several tables show large standard errors (e.g., TakeItBack-v0 baseline 0.42±0.24, ablation 'No LRU' 0.43±0.22), leaving some comparisons statistically fragile.

Despite the framing as solving 'RL problems,' all experiments are offline imitation learning; the abstract and title could mislead readers about the setting, and no online-RL or real-robot validation is provided (acknowledged, but it narrows the significance for the robotics audience).
Minor presentation issues: duplicated cross-references ('Figure 2, Figure 2'), duplicated sentence in A.8, and the abstract's 'Code and project page' left blank, all suggesting rushed preparation.
